blocks.x: The irony inherent to every moment of Salvation is difficult to miss, yet never played for laughs. Despite all this, he has somehow convinced himself that he is qualified to tell other people how to live.

Nicoll could have mined this premise primarily for comedy, but Salvation has something more uncomfortable in mind. Danny's contradictions expose the vulnerability of people who desperately want someone to tell them that their lives can become better, and the inherent contradictions of people who claim they have all the answers.

Danny himself is both a victim and an exploiter of that system. He pays some of his limited income to the man who trained him, effectively becoming another customer in the same cycle of self-improvement grifting that he later perpetuates. Once he starts working as a life coach, he encounters Scott (Stephen McMillan), a shy, disillusioned young man searching for direction while dealing with depression and a difficult relationship with his father.

Scott is exactly the kind of person who might be susceptible to Danny’s pitch. Danny speaks with complete conviction, presents himself as someone who understands the world, and has an easygoing friendliness that makes him seem trustworthy. He calls everyone “pal” and maintains an almost aggressively pleasant demeanor. But there is something subtly false about it all. His kindness feels rehearsed, and his confidence performative. The harder he tries to project success, the clearer it becomes that he is barely holding his own life together.

He exploits Scott’s uncertainty for his own financial benefit, becoming precisely the kind of manipulative figure he himself once paid to learn from. blocks.x: Liam Harkins makes Danny extraordinarily compelling, because he understands the character cannot simply be played as a traditional con artist. There needs to be enough genuine belief beneath the performance to explain why Danny is capable of convincing anyone, including himself. Stephen McMillan, meanwhile, provides an equally effective counterpoint as Scott.

Harkins finds the hollowness beneath every reassuring word, creating a character who is simultaneously personable and pathetic. Stephen McMillan, meanwhile, provides an equally effective counterpoint as Scott. Where Danny is loud, polished, and performatively confident, Scott is reserved and uncertain. McMillan gives the character a quiet vulnerability that makes his situation immediately affecting and, eventually, gut-wrenching to behold.

Nicoll's strongest achievement is turning Danny and Scott’s specific relationship into a broader examination of young men trying to figure out what comes next. Once people leave the structure of school and enter adulthood, the rules can suddenly become considerably less clear. What constitutes success? How does someone find purpose? What happens when the opportunities available to them don't match the life they imagined?

Those questions aren't uniquely Scottish, nor are they limited to men. But Salvation places them within a very recognizable Scottish environment, allowing the film to feel culturally specific without sacrificing its broader relevance. The desire to escape a stagnant life, find purpose, become successful, and believe that someone else has the blueprint for achieving it is practically universal. And all of these ideas are explored with nuance and sensitivity.
Salvation premiered at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival.
